title: AI rollback and incident closeout
summary: Use this playbook to contain an AI-related incident, restore the most recent verified acceptable state, validate recovery, and close the incident with auditable evidence.
prerequisites: Access to the incident record and available operational evidence
Authority to contain the affected AI function or contact someone who has that authority
A documented acceptable state, recovery procedure, or approved fallback

sections.title: Source correction and immediate answer
paragraphs: For an AI-related incident, contain the affected function, restore the most recent state that has evidence of acceptable behavior, validate that state against the incident symptoms and required controls, and close the incident only when recovery evidence, residual risk, decisions, and follow-up ownership are recorded. This is an intermediate-level playbook for practitioners and operators who already have access to an incident record and an approved recovery path.

The changed citation was content/resources/troubleshooting-operations/ai-rollback-and-incident-closeout.json. Its publisher was unregistered and the citation had never been verified, so it had passed its review cadence without establishing support for the guide. This update replaces that citation with the National Institute of Standards and Technology AI Risk Management Framework 1.0. The correction affects the source record and the guidance that depends on documented risk management, monitoring, response, recovery, and accountability. Material not affected by the citation correction is left unchanged.

sections.title: Rollback and closeout procedure
paragraphs: Step 1: Record the observed harm, degraded behavior, affected users or processes, detection time, and evidence already available. Preserve relevant records before changing the affected state. If the scope or severity cannot be established, keep the incident active, label unsupported details UNKNOWN in the incident record, restrict the affected function where authorized, and escalate to the person responsible for incident decisions.

Step 2: Contain the incident before attempting recovery. Stop the unsafe or unreliable path, limit access, or use an approved fallback according to the authority and procedures available to the response team. If containment fails or the team lacks authority, do not improvise an unapproved change; preserve the failure evidence, notify the responsible incident authority, and request the required access or intervention.

Step 3: Select the most recent candidate state for which there is evidence of acceptable behavior. Confirm what will change, what will remain in place, who approved the rollback, and how the original state can be preserved for investigation. If no candidate state has adequate evidence, do not guess; maintain containment and invoke the documented recovery or continuity process.

Step 4: Perform the rollback through the organization's approved change process and record the actor, approval, start time, completion time, affected scope, and resulting state. If execution fails, produces errors, or completes only partially, stop repeated attempts that could obscure evidence, preserve the observed result, return to containment where possible, and escalate through the documented recovery path.

Step 5: Validate recovery using the checks that define acceptable behavior for the affected function. Reproduce the incident trigger when it is safe to do so, check required safety and operational controls, compare current observations with the acceptable-state evidence, and inspect for unintended effects outside the original scope. If any required check fails or cannot be performed, keep the incident open, restore containment, record the failed or unavailable check, and reassess the recovery choice.

Step 6: Observe the recovered state for the monitoring period required by the organization's incident process. Record whether the original symptoms recur and whether new symptoms appear. If the incident recurs or monitoring is unavailable, return the incident to active response, contain the affected function, and assign restoration of monitoring or further diagnosis before closeout.

Step 7: Prepare closeout with the timeline, established impact, containment and rollback decisions, validation results, residual risk, retained evidence, and follow-up actions. Give each follow-up action an owner and a completion condition. If required evidence, approval, ownership, or validation is missing, do not mark the incident closed; record the missing item, assign the next action, and leave the incident open or pending under the organization's incident process.

sections.title: Expected evidence and verification
paragraphs: Expected evidence includes the incident record, preserved observations from before the rollback, containment and approval records, identification of the restored state, execution timestamps, validation results, monitoring observations, residual-risk decisions, and owned follow-up actions. Evidence should distinguish observed facts from details recorded as UNKNOWN.

Verify success by confirming that the affected function is in the approved recovered state, every required validation check passed, monitoring found no unresolved recurrence, and the incident record links each closeout decision to evidence and an accountable owner. If any condition is absent, the rollback or closeout is not yet verified; keep or return the incident to active or pending status and assign the missing validation, evidence collection, approval, or corrective action.
